- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model tends to underreact — increase forecast slightly to capture sentiment-driven momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤-0.2) and forecast is rising, model tends to overestimate — reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid overcorrection.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots in next 5–10 days — apply a “cool-down” correction: reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day for 3–5 days.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline after peak), model often fails to recognize — adjust forecast downward by 1–3% per day until trend reverses.
- If sentiment history shows repeated small positive signals (e.g., 0.00–0.20) and forecast is flat, model underestimates — add 0.5–1.0% to forecast to capture latent bullish bias.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the window (first 5–7 days) — apply a “lag correction”: reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% for first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating +/–0.2) and forecast is smooth, model misses volatility — introduce 0.5–1.0% jitter to forecast to reflect sentiment uncertainty.
